title: the burning
hook: a messenger gives the most powerful king in the world good advice, and the king answers by setting the messenger's tail on fire

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fight, part two. The young Aksha, the Brahmastra, and Hanuman choosing to stay bound to reach Ravana. Did you ask whether staying put served a bigger purpose? Today, the throne room. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Hanuman stands tied up before Ravana's throne, and the first thing Valmiki tells us is that Hanuman is impressed. Ravana is magnificent: radiant, crowned, mighty, surrounded by ministers. Hanuman thinks to himself that if this king weren't so unrighteous, he could be the guardian of heaven itself. It's a striking thought from the enemy's messenger. Then a minister asks him who sent him, and Hanuman answers. Not with threats. With counsel.
screen: `HANUMAN IS IMPRESSED.` → `IF ONLY HE WERE RIGHTEOUS.` → `NOT THREATS, COUNSEL.`

segments.voice: I am Sugriva's envoy, Hanuman says, and Rama's messenger. Then he speaks to Ravana as one would to a king who could still choose well. You know dharma, he says. You've gained great power through austerities. Don't throw it away for another man's wife. Give Sita back to Rama, and you can still live. That's Hanuman's counsel to Ravana: return her, and be saved. Ravana's answer is rage. Kill him, he orders. Then his younger brother Vibhishana speaks up. It is against dharma to kill a messenger, he says. Whatever an envoy says, you may punish him some other way, but you may not take his life. Ravana gives in, but grudgingly. A monkey's tail is precious to him, he says. Set it on fire. So they wrap Hanuman's tail in old cloth, soak it in oil, and light it, and parade him through the streets with drums, announcing his crime. The rakshasi guards run to tell Sita: the monkey you spoke with is being led through the city with his tail on fire. And Sita, in the grove, turns to the fire god, Agni. If I have served my husband faithfully, she prays, if I have any merit at all, be cool to Hanuman. And the fire, burning brightly on his tail, does not burn him. Hanuman is astonished. He feels the flame and no pain. He guesses it's Sita's doing, or Rama's power, or his father the wind's friendship with fire. Then he makes himself small, slips the ropes, grows huge again, and climbs to the rooftops, his tail still blazing.
screen: `RETURN SITA AND BE SAVED.` · `AN ENVOY MAY NOT BE KILLED.` · `SITA ASKS AGNI TO BE COOL.` · then, large: `THE FIRE DOES NOT BURN HIM.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone who might be going through a fire right now: a hard week, an illness, a trial. Sita couldn't go to Hanuman; she could only wish him well from where she was. Do the same. Hold that person in mind, and with each breath out, send them coolness, steadiness, ease. If you pray, you can offer them to God in your own way. The bell holds the time.
The burning. Ravana rejects Hanuman's counsel, Vibhishana saves the envoy's life, and Hanuman's tail is set alight, but Sita asks the fire to be cool, and it is.
Your line: the burning. Today, when someone you care about is in a hard place, send them coolness: a kind word, a check-in, or a quiet good wish. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: The burning of Hanuman's tail and Sita's prayer to Agni are familiar scenes in Ramayana retellings, and Vibhishana's rule that an envoy must not be killed is cited by some teachers as an example of dharma in war.

myth: Hanuman threatens Ravana from the start
he advises him to return Sita and save himself.
Vibhishana argues that killing an envoy is against dharma
so Ravana orders a different punishment.
Sita asks Agni to be cool to him, and the fire doesn't hurt.

fork.setup: you're Vibhishana. your brother the king orders an envoy killed. what do you say?
options: killing an envoy is against dharma; punish him another way.
fork.reveal: Vibhishana tells Ravana that an envoy must never be killed, whatever he says. Ravana settles for burning his tail.

original.note: Sanskrit agni, fire, and the god of fire, whom Sita asks to be cool.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hanuman's tail fire was just a punishment that backfired.
what it means: Sita, from the grove, asks the fire to spare him, and it does.

what a scholar hears: the principle that envoys are not to be killed (dūta-avadhya) appears in Indian texts on statecraft, and Valmiki puts it in Vibhishana's mouth, foreshadowing his later break with Ravana.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 49–51 (Hanuman before Ravana; his counsel)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 52 (Vibhishana on envoys)

notes: Hanuman's admiration of Ravana ('if he were not unrighteous he could be protector of the gods'): confirm Sundara 49.
Sita's appeal to Agni is described, not quoted, and the practice line offers prayer only as 'if you pray ... in your own way' (no new prayer is written). Confirm.
Hanuman's three guesses for the cool fire (Sita, Rama, his father's friendship with fire): confirm Sundara 53.
Trapdoor: the term dūta-avadhya and its use in statecraft literature; confirm.
